subject: forensic-medicine
title: Identification: Anthropometry, Cephalic Index and Craniofacial Superimposition

steps.title: The rise and historical fall of Bertillon anthropometry
steps.tx: Devised by French police clerk Alphonse Bertillon in 1879, the **Bertillon anthropometry identification system** (Bertillonage) represented the first scientific criminal identification framework. The system rested on the premises that human skeletal dimensions remain unchanged after age twenty-one, and that identical measurement combinations across eleven physical dimensions are astronomically rare. However, the system collapsed after the famous 1903 Will West case exposed measurement discrepancies.
steps.say: Bertillonage was the first scientific identification system, recording eleven body measurements. It was abandoned after the Will West case proved fingerprints superior.

Fingerprints proved completely unique and non-varying

steps.tx: In 1879 the French police clerk Alphonse Bertillon built the **Bertillon anthropometry identification system**, the first scientific scheme for naming criminals. It assumed that bone measurements stop changing after age twenty one and that the same set of eleven dimensions almost never repeats. Clerks recorded those lengths with calipers. The method failed after the 1903 Will West case, when two men shared nearly the same measurements and fingerprints proved the safer identifier.
steps.say: Bertillonage recorded eleven body measurements on the belief that adult bones do not change and combinations rarely match. The Will West case in 1903 showed two men could share those lengths, and fingerprints replaced the system.

steps.title: The eleven standard Bertillon physical measurements
steps.tx: Under the Bertillonage protocol, criminal clerks recorded **eleven standardized body measurements** using sliding calipers and gauges. These comprised standing height, sitting height, arm span (reach), head length, head breadth, bizygomatic facial breadth, length of right ear, length of left foot, length of left middle finger, length of left little finger, and length of left forearm from elbow to fingertip (cubit).
steps.say: Bertillon recorded standing and sitting height, arm span, head length and breadth, ear length, left foot, middle finger, little finger, and forearm cubit.

steps.tx: Clerks using Bertillonage recorded **eleven standardized body measurements** with sliding calipers and gauges. The list was standing height, sitting height, arm span, head length, head breadth, bizygomatic facial breadth, right ear length, left foot length, left middle finger length, left little finger length, and the left forearm cubit from elbow to fingertip. Head length, the measurement in view, was only one cell in that grid. No single caliper reading identified the person. The combination was the claim.
steps.say: Bertillon measured standing and sitting height, arm span, head length and breadth, face breadth, right ear, left foot, left middle and little fingers, and left forearm. Head length was one of those eleven lengths, not an identity by itself.

steps.title: The Will West case and triumph of dactylography
steps.tx: The historic downfall of anthropometry occurred in the **Will West penitentiary incident** at Leavenworth Prison in 1903. An incoming prisoner named Will West matched the exact eleven anthropometric measurements and photographic portrait of an existing inmate named William West, despite having no known biological relation. When fingerprint impressions were obtained, their friction ridge minutiae were entirely dissimilar, prompting criminal bureaus worldwide to replace Bertillonage with dactylography.
steps.say: In 1903, two unrelated prisoners had identical Bertillon measurements and facial features, but completely different fingerprints, cementing dactylography's supremacy.

right.title: Galton-Henry dactylography

Completely independent of examiner measuring pressure

steps.title: Cranial anthropometry and the cephalic index
steps.tx: In physical anthropology and racial identification, the **cephalic index cranial calculation** (devised by Anders Retzius) expresses the ratio between maximum transverse cranial breadth and maximum anteroposterior cranial length. Measured using spreading calipers from the glabella to inion, and across the maximum biparietal width, the cephalic index equals maximum breadth divided by maximum length multiplied by one hundred.
steps.say: The cephalic index equals maximum head breadth divided by length times one hundred, measured with spreading calipers between glabella and inion.

Measurement of maximum head breadth: Biparietal width

steps.title: Classification of skull types by cephalic index
steps.tx: Based on the calculated index, physical anthropologists classify crania into **three primary cephalic categories**. Dolichocephalic (long/narrow) skulls feature an index under seventy-five, typical of pure Aryans, Dravidians, and African populations. Mesaticephalic (medium) skulls range from seventy-five to seventy-nine-point-nine, typical of Europeans. Brachycephalic (broad/round) skulls score eighty or above, characteristic of Mongolian, Chinese, and Alpine populations.
steps.say: Skulls are classified by cephalic index: dolichocephalic under seventy-five, mesocephalic seventy-five to eighty, and brachycephalic over eighty.

rows: Western Europeans, modern North Indians, Anglo-Saxons
Mongolians, Chinese, Nepalese, Swiss Alpine groups

steps.title: Principles of craniofacial superimposition
steps.tx: When an unknown skeletonized skull is recovered, **photographic craniofacial superimposition** compares the skull directly against antemortem facial photographs of missing persons. First utilized in the historic Ruxton murder trial (1935), the technique mounts the cleaned skull on an adjustable craniophore, rotating it until its orientation, tilt, and optical distance precisely duplicate the subject's head position in life.
steps.say: Craniofacial superimposition aligns an unknown skull on a craniophore with life photographs of a missing person, matching anatomical bony landmarks.

nodes.label: Antemortem life photograph of missing person enlarged to life size

steps.tx: An unknown skull can be compared with a missing person photograph by **photographic craniofacial superimposition**. The cleaned skull is fixed on an adjustable craniophore and turned until orientation, tilt, and camera distance copy the head position in life. Bony landmarks are then checked against the portrait. The method was first used in the Ruxton murder trial of 1935 and still serves when only a skeletonised head remains.
steps.say: The skull is mounted on a craniophore and aligned with a life photograph so tilt and distance match. Landmark agreement, first argued in the Ruxton trial of 1935, supports identity.

steps.title: Anatomical landmarks in superimposition analysis
steps.tx: Pathologists evaluate concordance across standardized **craniofacial anthropometric landmarks**, comparing bony contours with overlying soft tissues. Critical landmarks comprise the nasion (nasofrontal junction), glabella, prosthion (upper alveolar margin), gnathion (inferior chin border), orbital rims matching pupillary apertures, ectocanthion, endocanthion, and lateral nasal aperture margins matching nasal ala contours. Facial tissue thickness tables guide expected soft tissue depth.
steps.say: The pathologist matches landmarks like nasion, chin gnathion, eye sockets, and nasal aperture, ensuring soft tissue depths match anatomical charts.

rows: Eyeballs must sit centered within orbital cavities
Bony nasal spine must support cartilaginous columella
Teeth must correspond with visible smile line
Soft tissue chin pad thickness must match norms

steps.title: Video and digital 3D computed superimposition
steps.tx: Modern forensic laboratories replace manual optical mirrors with **digital video superimposition technology**. The skull is scanned using multi-detector computed tomography to create a three-dimensional surface mesh. Computer algorithms rotate the virtual skull model, align facial landmark vectors, adjust opacity sliders dynamically, and fade between the bony skull and antemortem life photograph, detecting subtle discrepancies that exclude wrong candidates.
steps.say: Modern labs use 3D CT skull scans and computer fading software to rotate and superimpose the skull over family photographs with millimeter accuracy.

steps.title: Evidentiary value: Exclusion versus positive proof
steps.tx: In legal medicine, courts treat the **evidentiary value of superimposition** primarily as a definitive method of exclusion rather than absolute positive proof. If anatomical landmarks, teeth, or orbital shapes fail to align with the photograph, the skull is conclusively excluded from belonging to that individual. However, because unrelated skulls of similar build can simulate a match, positive identity requires confirmation through nuclear or mitochondrial DNA analysis.
steps.say: Superimposition conclusively rules out wrong persons, but positive identification requires confirmation with dental records or DNA profiling.
